name: t0009
content:
# Meta-Token Specification — Ghost-AOS Git-Bus Treaty, Clause MTX-1

## 1. Core principle

The anchor carries **only** the meaning. Nothing derived from any token set ever enters the anchor's bytes. Token sets live in a separate, mutable, per-set binding layer that points **at** anchors. This is what makes byte-identity across sets provable rather than hoped for: every consumer terminates at the same immutable object and verifies its hash. Binding tables locate the anchor; they never touch the emitted bytes.

## 2. Object formats (exact bytes)

### 2.1 Anchor object (immutable, content-addressed)

Stored in the bus ODB exactly like a git loose object:

```
raw      = b"anchor " + ascii(decimal_len(body)) + b"\x00" + body
stored   = zlib_deflate(raw)
path     = objects/<hex(A)[0:2]>/<hex(A)[2:]>, file mode 0444
A        = sha256(raw)            # 32 bytes; 64 hex chars canonical, ≥16-hex abbreviations allowed
```

`body` is **canonical CBOR** (RFC 8949 §4.2.1: definite lengths only, shortest-form integer heads, keys sorted bytewise on their encoded form, UTF-8 strings, **floats forbidden**):

```
{"kind":"anchor", "spec":<CBOR>, "v":1}
```

Note what is *absent*: generator, generation counter, timestamps, per-set spans. Any such field would fork the anchor per producer. Anchors are add-only; the state machine is `ABSENT → REGISTERED` (terminal). No deregister op exists.

### 2.2 Lexicon (per token set, mutable, git-versioned)

Path `lex/<set_id>.cbor`, also canonical CBOR:

```
{"bindings":[{"a":<32-byte A>,"t":[uint,...],"span":[uint,uint]|null}, ...],
 "enc":"<fingerprint of tokenizer params>", "rev":<uint>, "set_id":"<str>"}
```

Invariant: `bindings` sorted ascending by `a`; within one set, the map `t → a` is **injective** (enforced at write time, error 21). `span` is advisory and excluded from the anchor — spans differ per set by construction.

### 2.3 Index

`anchors.idx`: fixed 36-byte records `raw_A(32) ‖ be_u32(offset into anchors.log)`. `anchors.log`: one canonical-JSON anchor body per line, audit trail.

## 3. State change: `REGISTER_ANCHOR(spec_bytes, bindings)`

Pre-state: `refs/treaty/head → C_n`; tree holds `anchors.idx`, `anchors.log`, N lexicons; K anchor objects in ODB.

1. `body = cbor_canonical({"kind":"anchor","spec":cbor_canonical(spec),"v":1})`
2. `A = sha256(b"anchor "+len(body)+b"\x00"+body)`
3. **Idempotence gate**: if object exists ∧ index contains `A` → return `hex(A)`, exit 0, **zero bytes changed anywhere**, ref unmoved.
4. Write loose object (mode 0444).
5. Per `(set_id, t)`: insert `{"a":A,"t":t,"span":null}` preserving sort; bump `rev`. Violations abort atomically: 21 = injectivity clash, 14 = empty `t`, 22 = unknown set, 12 = non-canonical bytes (dup keys, indefinite lengths, floats, unsorted).
6. Append index record + log line.
7. Commit `register-anchor <hex(A)>`, parent `C_n`, fast-forward `refs/treaty/head` under `head.lock`.

Post-state delta, exactly: ODB `+1` object; `anchors.idx` `+36` bytes; `anchors.log` `+1` line; each touched lexicon `+1` binding, `rev+1`; one new commit.

## 4. Resolution ops (determinism contract)

- `RESOLVE(set, tokens)`: **exact-match only** — input sequence must equal some `bindings[i].t`; yields `A`; fetch object at `path(A)`; recompute `sha256` and compare (fail-closed, exit 7 on mismatch). Emit `body.spec` bytes verbatim.
- `SEGMENT(set, stream)`: greedy longest-match, left to right; ties broken by smallest anchor ID. Deterministic given the sort order.
- `MATERIALIZE(anchor_ref) → tokens_of(set)`: reverse lookup.

**Treaty clause T-1:** for all sets `S, T` and all `A ∈ dom(S) ∩ dom(T)`:
`materialize(resolve(S,σ)) ≡ materialize(resolve(T,τ))` byte-for-byte, where σ, τ are the registered sequences for `A`.
Proof obligation: both paths reduce to reading one hash-verified immutable object; lexica affect only *locating* `A`, never the output bytes.

Wire form between peers: `MTX1:<64hex>`; receivers fetch-by-hash and MUST re-verify before use.

## 5. Acceptance test `T-BYTEID-001`

Three deliberately incompatible sets: S1 = raw byte tokens, S2 = arbitrary word IDs, S3 = merged multi-token IDs. Spec (fixed fixture, hex):

```
spec_hex = a2636f70610166656d69740267...   # {"op":"emit","text":"ghost-bus/α"}
```

Bindings:
```
S1: [103,104,111,115,116,45,98,117,115,47,206,177]
S2: [7741]
S3: [512,88,12007]
```

```sh
# 1 — register; capture A
A=$(bus register-anchor --spec spec.cbor \
      --bind tok/byte8@1:103,104,111,115,116,45,98,117,115,47,206,177 \
      --bind tok/word32k@2:7741 \
      --bind tok/bpe-mix@1:512,88,12007)          # stdout: 64-hex + \n

# 2 — idempotent replay
A2=$(bus register-anchor --spec spec.cbor ...same args...)
assert "$A" = "$A2"
assert "$(git -C bus.git rev-parse refs/treaty/head)" unchanged   # true no-op

# 3 — resolve from every entry point; compare bytes
for s in tok/byte8@1 tok/word32k@2 tok/bpe-mix@1; do
  bus resolve --from "$s" --tokens <registered seq> --emit spec > "r_${s//\//_}.bin"
done
cmp r_tok_byte8_1.bin r_tok_word32k_2.bin
cmp r_tok_word32k_2.bin r_tok_bpe_mix_1.bin                     # both must exit 0

# 4 — reverse: materialize per set reproduces registration inputs
for s in ...all three...; do
  bus materialize --anchor "$A" --to "$s" > m.json
  assert m.json tokens == original binding for $s
done

# 5 — insertion-order independence (fresh clone)
# register in order S3, S1, S2 → identical $A
assert "$A_ord" = "$A"

# 6 — integrity is hash-enforced, not table-trusted
cp objects/${A:0:2}/${A:2} /tmp/corrupt
printf '\xff' | dd of=/tmp/corrupt bs=1 seek=10 conv=notrunc
bus resolve --from tok/byte8@1 ... --odb-shadow /tmp/corrupt
assert $? = 7                                                    # fail closed

# 7 — injectivity guard rolls back atomically
bus register-anchor --spec other.cbor --bind tok/word32k@2:7741
assert $? = 21
assert head unmoved && lex/tok-word32k@2.cbor rev unchanged
```

Golden-vector pinning: `vectors/T-BYTEID-001.json` ships the reference `A` and the three materialized binaries, regenerated by `make vectors` from the reference implementation; CI asserts byte-equality against them.

**Pass criterion:** steps 1–5 produce byte-identical outputs across all sets and both registration orders; step 6 exits 7; step 7 exits 21 with provably zero side effects. Together these establish: one anchor ID independent of set count/order, identical emitted bytes from every set, identity enforced by digest, and replay safety.
reasoning:
The user is asking me to design a concrete mechanism: a "meta-token" in something called the "Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty." This appears to be a fictional/speculative system — there's no real standard called "Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty." The user is treating this as a hard design problem and wants:

1. A content-addressed anchor (meta-token) that resolves meaning across multiple token sets
2. The exact state change / data shape
3. An acceptance test that proves byte-identity
4. Concrete, exact, grounded, no fluff

So I need to invent/design a rigorous specification as if I'm the "thousand-ask mining engine" doing real engineering work. Let me think about what this system would plausibly be.

"Ghost-AOS git-bus treaty": sounds like a protocol where agents/systems ("AOS" = agent operating system?) exchange tokens over a git-backed bus. A "treaty" implies a contract between parties about how tokens are interpreted. The core problem: different token sets (different vocabularies, different encoders, different model tokenizers) need to resolve to the same meaning via one anchor. The anchor is content-addressed — i.e., its identity is derived from its own bytes (hash), like git objects.

Key insight from git: git object IDs are SHA-1 (now SHA-256) over `"<type> <len>\0<content>"`. Content-addressing gives immutability and deduplication. The meta-token should be exactly that: an immutable object whose ID binds it.

But the hard part stated: "one content-addressed anchor resolving meaning across multiple token sets." Meaning: the same meta-token must resolve identically regardless of which token set (tokenizer/vocabulary/encoding scheme) a consumer uses. So the resolution function must be deterministic per token set but converge on the same semantic object.

Let me design this concretely.

### Design

**Meta-token object** (git-style blob with a typed header):

```
MTX1 <payload_len>\0 <canonical_payload>
```

Where:
- `MTX1` = meta-token format version 1
- canonical payload is CBOR or canonical JSON with fixed key ordering

The meta-token ID: `sha256("mtx1\0" + canonical_bytes)` truncated to 32 hex chars? Or full 64. Git uses full hash; short forms are display only. Keep full 256-bit for treaty purposes; allow abbreviated refs at 16+ hex chars with uniqueness check.

Canonical payload fields:
```cbor
{
  "v": 1,
  "sets": { "<set-id>": [seq of ints], ... },   # per token-set surface encoding
  "sem": <semantic digest>,                      # hash of resolved semantics
  "canon": "<canonical text>"                    # optional human-readable canonical form
}
```

Wait — but if we embed all token sets inside the anchor, then adding a new token set changes the anchor's content → new ID. That breaks "one anchor across sets." Two options:

Option A: Anchor = pure semantic core (set-independent). Token-set bindings live in *separate* ref objects that point to the anchor. Then "resolving meaning across multiple token sets" = each set has a binding table mapping its local tokens → anchor ID, and the anchor resolves back through any binding.

This is cleaner and mirrors git: blobs are content-addressed; refs are mutable pointers. The meta-token anchor never mutates; per-set lexicons are the mutable layer.

Option B: Anchor includes a merkle root of all set-bindings; adding a set issues a new anchor version, chained. More complex.

Option A is right. Let me spec it fully.

**Data shapes**

1. **Anchor object (immutable, content-addressed)** — stored in the bus repo under `objects/<first2>/<rest>` exactly like git loose objects, zlib-deflated:

   Raw bytes before hashing:
   ```
   "anchor\0" || u32be(len) || body
   ```
   
   Hmm, better to mirror git exactly: `"anchor " + decimal(len) + "\0" + body`. That makes it drop-in for a git odb if desired.
   
   Body = canonical CBOR map, keys sorted by length-then-lexicographic (RFC 8949 canonical CBOR: bytewise lexicographic of encoded keys):
   
   ```
   {
     "alg": "sha2-256",          # hash alg used for self-ID
     "sem": bstr,                # 32-byte semantic commitment = sha256(canonical semantic payload)
     "spec": bstr,               # canonical semantic payload itself (the meaning), CBOR
     "ttl": uint                 # treaty epoch / generation counter
   }
   ```
   
   Actually — do we store `sem` separately from `spec`? If `spec` is present, `sem` is derivable. Redundant. But the redundancy is the point: `sem` is what gets *referenced* in signatures and cross-repo links so that a consumer can verify without carrying full spec... no, verification requires recomputation which needs spec anyway. Drop `sem`; the anchor's object ID IS the semantic address. Simpler:

   Body:
   ```
   {
     "v": 1,
     "kind": "anchor",
     "spec": { ... canonical meaning ... },
     "gen": <uint treaty generation>
   }
   ```
   
   Hmm, including `gen` in the content means the same meaning at two generations = two anchors. Is that desired? Treaty generations might change interpretation rules. If gen affects interpretation, it belongs in the content (two anchors genuinely differ). If not, exclude. I'll say: exclude `gen` from anchor; generations live in the bus commit history. Anchor = pure meaning. That maximizes cross-set/cross-time stability. Good.

   So anchor body:
   ```
   {"kind":"anchor","spec":<CBOR>,"v":1}
   ```
   Canonical CBOR: definite-length maps, shortest-form integer heads, keys sorted bytewise on encoded form. Deterministic per RFC 8949 §4.2.1.

   Anchor ID: `A = sha256("anchor " + len(body) + "\0" + body)` — wait, include the header in the hash, git-style. Yes: hash covers header+body, so the ID commits to both type tag and length. Full 32 bytes, hex 64 chars. Display abbreviations ≥16 hex.

2. **Token-set binding table (mutable, per set, versioned by git commit)**

   Each participating token set `S` (identified by `set_id`, e.g., `"tok/gpt-bpe-r50k@2024-01"` or `"tok/sentencepiece-32k@v3"`) maintains:
   
   ```
   lex/<set_id>.cbor : {
     "set_id": str,
     "enc": {"name": ..., "params_digest": sha256 of tokenizer params},
     "map": [
       // entries sorted by anchor ID ascending (bytewise)
       {"a": bstr(32),        # anchor id raw bytes
        "t": array<uint>,     # token id sequence in THIS set covering the canonical span
        "span": [uint,uint]}  # byte offsets [start,end) into canonical text (optional but recommended)
     ]
   }
   ```

   Resolution direction A (tokens→meaning): tokenize input with S's encoder → sequence of ints → longest-prefix match against `map[*].t` (entries indexed by first token id via hash index) → candidate anchor IDs → verify by re-hashing anchor object fetched from odb (`objects/ab/cdef…`). Verified ⇒ meaning resolved.

   Resolution direction B (meaning→tokens): anchor ID → fetch anchor → look up `map` entry where `a == A` → emit `t` sequence for set S.

3. **Bus state change (the exact mutation)**

   The git-bus is a bare repo; the treaty's state lives at ref `refs/treaty/head`. A state change is one commit appending to a log file plus updating odb objects. Concretely, registering a meta-token:

   Pre-state:
   - `refs/treaty/head` → commit C_n whose tree contains:
     - `anchors.idx`: append-only binary index: records of 36 bytes: `[a(32) | u32be(offset)]` into `anchors.log`
     - `anchors.log`: newline-delimited canonical JSON/CBOR lines of anchor bodies (so history survives even after gc prunes? actually odb holds them; log is for audit)
     - `lex/<set_id>.cbor` per registered set
   - odb: anchor objects absent/present

   Operation `REGISTER_ANCHOR(spec_bytes, bindings)` where bindings = list of `(set_id, token_seq)`:

   Step 1. Build body: canonical_cbor({"kind":"anchor","spec":canonical_cbor(spec),"v":1})
   Step 2. Compute `A = sha256(header||body)`.
   Step 3. Idempotence check: if `objects/A[0:2]/A[2:]` exists AND `anchors.idx` contains `A` → return existing anchor ID, no-op (state unchanged, exit code 0, output identical bytes).
   Step 4. Write loose object: zlib(`"anchor "+len+"\0"+body`) at path above, mode 0444.
   Step 5. For each `(set_id, t)`: append entry `{"a":A,"t":t,"span":null}` to `lex/<set_id>.cbor`, keeping sort invariant by anchor ID; update the set's `rev` counter field. Reject (exit 21, atomic abort) if `t` collides with an existing entry mapping to a *different* anchor in the same set (one token-sequence → at most one anchor per set; injectivity enforced per set).
   Step 6. Append index record `A||offset` to `anchors.idx`; append line to `anchors.log`.
   Step 7. Commit tree with message `register-anchor <hex(A)>`; parent C_n → child C_{n+1}; fast-forward `refs/treaty/head`.

   Atomicity: steps 4–7 in one transaction; on any failure, delete written objects, truncate appends, no ref move. Use lockfile `refs/treaty/head.lock`.

   The inverse op `DEREGISTER` doesn't exist — anchors are permanent once committed (content-addressed immutability); deprecation is done by tombstone entry `{a:A,"dead":<commit>}` in idx? Keep simple: anchors are add-only. State machine: ABSENT → REGISTERED (terminal). No other transitions.

4. **Resolution determinism requirement** (the actual hard part): the same anchor must yield byte-identical resolution outputs regardless of which set is used as the entry point. Define:

   `resolve(entry_set, tokens) → A` must be a total function: for any valid token sequence bound in set S, the returned A equals the A bound at registration time, forever, because (a) lex tables are append-only within a set, (b) collisions rejected, (c) anchors immutable. Byte-identity claim: the canonical semantic bytes emitted by `materialize(A)` are identical across all consumers since they re-derive from the same odb object.

5. **Acceptance test proving byte-identity**

   Test name: `T-BYTEID-001`. Setup: three token sets with deliberately incompatible encodings:
   - S1: ASCII byte tokens (ids = byte values)
   - S2: word-level ids assigned arbitrarily
   - S3: BPE-ish merges producing multi-token sequences

   Register one anchor with spec = canonical CBOR of `{"op":"emit","text":"ghost-bus/α"}` (note non-ASCII to catch encoding drift).

   Procedure:
   1. `bus register-anchor --spec spec.cbor --bind S1:[103,104,111,115,116,45,98,117,115,47,206,177] --bind S2:[7741] --bind S3:[512,88,12007]` → capture stdout hex `A`.
   2. Re-run identical command → assert stdout byte-identical AND `refs/treaty/head` unchanged (idempotent no-op).
   3. For each Si: `bus resolve --from Si --tokens <seq> --emit canonical` → write to files r1..r3.
   4. Assert `cmp r1 r2 && cmp r2 r3` → zero exit, i.e., byte-identical materialized payloads.
   5. Round-trip: `bus materialize --anchor A --to Si` for each i → t_i sequences equal registration inputs.
   6. Corruption probe: flip one byte in a copy of anchor object → `resolve` MUST fail with exit 7 (digest mismatch), never silently resolve — proves identity is enforced by hash, not by table lookup alone.
   7. Cross-order: register bindings in order S3,S1,S2 in a fresh clone → identical A. Proves A independent of insertion order/set count.

   Pass criterion: all asserts pass and `sha256(r1)==sha256(r2)==sha256(r3)` printed equal; plus step 6 nonzero-exit verified.

Also worth specifying the wire format for transmitting the anchor between nodes: `MTX1<A-hex>` inline reference, expansion rules, and the rule that a peer receiving unknown A requests the object over the bus (fetch by hash, verify).

Let me also nail down canonical CBOR details so "byte-identical" is actually achievable:
- Integers: shortest head (uint ≤23 → single byte; ≤255 → 0x18xx; etc.)
- Map keys: sorted bytewise by their CBOR encoding (length-first for equal prefixes — RFC 8949 says length-first then bytewise; canonical per §4.2.1 is bytewise lexicographic of the encoded key)
- Strings: UTF-8, definite length
- No floats needed; forbid them (reject with exit 12 if present) to dodge NaN/-0 nondeterminism
- Indefinite lengths forbidden

Hash domain separation: header string `"anchor "` distinguishes from future types (`"lexicon "`, `"tombstone "`).

Edge cases to state:
- Empty token sequence: legal, maps to empty-spec anchor? Disallow — reject empty `t` (exit 14).
- Same tokens→same anchor in one set: fine (re-registration no-op).
- Same anchor, two sets, different spans: spans are advisory, excluded from anchor content (they'd break cross-set identity).
- Abbreviation collision: resolving by 16-hex prefix requires unambiguous match else exit 8.

Now the acceptance test needs exact expected bytes. Give concrete example numbers. Let me construct a small worked example with actual plausible hashes — I can't compute sha256 mentally, so instead of fabricating fake hashes as if real, give the test as executable pseudo-shell with assertions, and specify that expected A is captured from a known-good vector included in the treaty test vectors file `vectors/T-BYTEID-001.json` containing precomputed A for the given spec bytes. Actually for concreteness I can present the spec bytes in hex and note the fixture ships with the precomputed digest. Better: make the assertion structural (equality across runs/sets) rather than depending on a magic constant, plus one pinned vector. I'll pin a vector placeholder clearly labeled as fixture-computed. Hmm, "no hedging" — but fabricating a specific sha256 value would be wrong/fabrication. Structural equality assertions ARE the proof of byte-identity; the pinned vector just guards regressions. I'll include the exact spec hex and describe the pinned value as computed at fixture-generation time by the reference implementation, giving the command to regenerate it. That's honest and concrete.

Actually, let me reconsider: can I give a real sha256? I cannot reliably compute sha256 by hand. So the correct engineering answer: the test compares outputs against each other and against a checked-in golden vector generated by the reference tool. That's standard practice (like git's own test vectors). Fine.

Format of the answer: structured spec sections — object formats with byte layouts, state transition (before/after of refs/treaty/head tree + odb), ops with error codes, determinism contract, then the acceptance test as an executable script with assertions. Keep it tight, dense, concrete. Use code blocks. Headers help navigation here. Length: substantial but no padding — every line load-bearing.

Let me draft the byte layouts precisely.

Anchor loose object path: `objects/a3/1f…` using hex(A). File content = zlib-deflate(`b"anchor " + ascii(len(body)) + b"\x00" + body`). A = sha256(that uncompressed header+body). Matches git convention so a stock git odb could host these as custom-typed objects.

Lexicon file: canonical CBOR too, so diffs are meaningful and byte-stable:
```
{"bindings":[{...}],"enc":"<set encoder fingerprint>","rev":N,"set_id":"..."}
```
Keys sorted: "bindings","enc","rev","set_id" — bytewise: b=0x62..., e,r,s → bindings < enc < rev < set_id ✓.

Index record: 36 bytes fixed: `bytes(A)[32] || be_u32(log_offset)`.

State snapshot before/after REGISTER:

Before:
```
refs/treaty/head → C_n
tree(C_n): anchors.idx(36·k bytes), anchors.log(k lines), lex/S1.cbor, lex/S2.cbor
odb: k anchor objects
```
After (success):
```
refs/treaty/head → C_{n+1}, parent C_n
tree diff: anchors.idx +36 bytes, anchors.log +1 line, lex/Si.cbor updated (+1 binding each, rev+1)
odb: +1 object at objects/A[:2]/A[2:] mode 444
```
No-op path: nothing changes anywhere; exit 0; stdout = hex(A)+"\n".

Error codes: 
- 7 digest mismatch on read
- 8 ambiguous abbreviation
- 12 non-canonical bytes (float/indefinite/dup-key/unsorted)
- 14 empty binding
- 21 injectivity violation (token seq already → different anchor in that set)
- 22 missing referenced set

Determinism contract (the treaty clause): For all sets S,T and all A∈dom(S)∩dom(T): `materialize(resolve(S,σ)) == materialize(resolve(T,τ))` byte-for-byte whenever σ,τ are the registered sequences for A in S,T. Proof sketch: both paths terminate at fetching the unique object at path derived from A and verifying sha256 — the bytes compared come from one immutable source; lex tables influence only *locating* A, never the emitted bytes. That's the crux: keep the meaning out of the mutable layer entirely.

Wire form: `MTX1:<64hex>` inline; peers fetch-by-hash; a node MAY cache but MUST re-verify hash on use (cheap, 32B context).

Acceptance test script — write as POSIX-ish shell with a tiny python helper for CBOR? Keep it as `bus` CLI calls + `cmp`/`sha256sum` + explicit asserts. Include the corruption probe and order-independence probe. Also negative tests: duplicate binding to different anchor → exit 21, and state rolled back (head unmoved).

I think also define `resolve` matching algorithm precisely to avoid ambiguity: exact-sequence match only (no fuzzy/prefix absorption). Input tokens are matched against `map` entries by exact equality of the int array; if input contains a registered sequence as contiguous subsequence, replace occurrences left-to-right greedily longest-match? Simpler treaty rule: RESOLVE operates on a whole input sequence only if it equals a registered sequence exactly; SEGMENT operation does greedy longest-match left-to-right for embedding anchors inside larger streams. Define both, one sentence each. Greedy longest match is deterministic given sort order by length desc then anchor asc. Specify tie-break: among equal-length candidates pick smallest anchor id. Deterministic ✓.

Byte-identity proof obligation for the acceptance test: the test demonstrates (i) same A across orders/sets, (ii) identical materialized bytes across all three sets, (iii) hash-enforced integrity (corruption fails closed), (iv) idempotent replay. That's the full claim.

One more thing: "multiple token sets" may also mean multiple *versions* of a tokenizer over time. Covered: set_id includes version; old lex files remain; anchors persist. Migration = register new set bindings to same A.

Length/format: This deserves a thorough, well-structured technical spec. Markdown headers, code blocks, tables minimal. Aim ~900–1300 words equivalent with code blocks. Dense, zero fluff.
